p: What are the factors that you consider when determining whether an intersection or school is going to get a crossing guard? I'm sure foot traffic, as well as the vehicle collision rate, but is there anything else?

So we don't just do collision data, because that would be reactive. So we'd like to be proactive. And pedestrian volume, if you have a lot of people attending that school and there's a lot of pedestrians crossing, traffic volume, is there a lot of cars coming through? Speed conditions, is it a wide open street where vehicles can get up in speed? What type of crossing is it? Is there traffic crossing/traffic/signals at the place

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 180 Committee on Public Safety that can help mitigate the dangers, sight distance — are there a lot of turning vehicles? Then, when we look at students’ age, we tend to really prioritize elementary and junior high schools. And then we look at collision data. Collision data is a metric we use to see how we're doing as a whole. So if you look at pedestrian youth, this is 17 years or younger, pedestrian juveniles, 17 years or younger, between the start of the school year, September 1st, 2025, to April 19, 2026, between the hours of 7:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., to school hours, we're down in juvenile pedestrians being struck and injured by a vehicle, 13%. So that's a metric that we use as a barometer to see if we are doing well with our deployment. It's strategic. We're basing it on this data — and our assessments from our commanding officers, our coordinators, or Level II. So we're getting a lot of feedback about where and how we deploy.
Do we have any data on the number of school crossing requests that have gone unaddressed?

That I don't have.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 181 Committee on Public Safety
Also, just thinking about the daily manpower of the School Crossing Guard Division, approximately 2,300. How many school crossing guards are called out on an average day or week?
Yeah, that's a question that I've been hearing you ask, and I have to get back to you on that one. I don't have that.
Okay. Even if we don't have data, is that an issue that we've heard about with them not showing up?

So, Level I is part-time employees who get paid an hourly salary. We could probably track that. But I'd have to look at the Level II, who are salaried employees. With Level I, if you don't work your 20 hours, it can contractually cause you issues as far as coverage, medical coverage specifically. I don't know if calling out is an issue, but I'd have to get back to you.

How many school crossing guards work less than 20 hours? Is that the entire 2,219, or is there-- because I know less than 20 hours they don't qualify for benefits.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 182 Committee on Public Safety
So, 2,219 are all the Level I guards. Those are the ones that you see on a daily basis in the crosswalks. They're the ones who get paid the hourly rate.
Yeah, and how many of those work less than 20 hours?
That I would have to get back to that analysis.
Okay. How many school crossing guards, based on-- and I know there's, again, not that much data on given a request that you get, but I think we could agree that it's a lot of requests.
Yeah.

Just curious, what would be a number that you think would get us to a better point when it comes to addressing these requests that students, parents, or school educators are making for school crossing guards? What would be a number that would put us in a very good position on this issue?

I'll just go back to this — in 2018, we had 2,500 school crossing guards. That was 340 more than we were today. On our publicly

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 183 Committee on Public Safety displayed database, where you see our posts, I want to say the number was 2,639. So, I'll let you make that assessment. Those are the factual numbers.
Thank you for that information. Do we have any data on incidents, traffic-related incidents that have happened in the high-risk intersections around schools?

Yeah, that's a great question. Let me just start off by saying, on October 20th, 2023, a 13-year veteran, 63 years of age, Krystyna Naprawa, a school crossing guard, was killed in a line of duty while she was crossing a family in Woodhaven, Queens. Tragic. She was beloved, and it was painful for the Department. We came together as a department and assessed what happened. We had a six-day training prior to that for school crossing guards to talk about how to mitigate traffic and how to deal with aggressive drivers, conflict management, hazard recognition, use of hand signals, and making eye contact with drivers before stepping out into an intersection. And then we enhance that training following her tragic death. An extra day, and we analyzed the equipment that was given to school crossing guards. Typically, their uniforms are

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 184 Committee on Public Safety reflective, every part of them, including the hat and the gloves. But we doubled down, we gave them what we call stop paddles along with a six-foot pole extension to make them more visible. Because one of the analyses, when this happened, we determined that it was a truck that struck her, and the visibility of the school crossing guard was not readily apparent. So our priority as the Chief of Patrol's office, who oversees the school crossing guards, is to keep them safe. So we revamped our training. So we do have incidents, tragic incidents at school crossings, and that's one that hurts.

Okay. Thank you for the information. And last question before I pass it to Council Member Phil Wong. And the same question that I asked about the School Safety Agents, what would you say are the top three needs to fully stabilize the school Crossing Guard Division — budgetary needs, headcount, anything and everything legislative, operational needs? What would put the School Crossing Guard Division in a much better position, given the many things that people come to us with concerns and requirements, and et cetera? Paying them is, I'm sure, one of them, what else?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 185 Committee on Public Safety

Again, the training and the support for these school crossing guards. I know the school system and the principals and the employees praise these school crossing guards, and we get a lot of positive feedback from the community. So that's very helpful. I'll keep drilling home that we have 2,639 posts displayed on our public website. Our headcount in 2018 was 340 more than it is today. We're currently running at our allocation number — at or about. So I'll just say that. And then lastly, I know the questions are always about pay. Obviously, that will improve retention and hiring, but that is a question beyond my scope.
Okay. And what's the total budget for the school crossing guard?

Sure. So, based on our current budgeted headcount numbers, the actual dollars associated with the school Crossing Guard Program are roughly $49.3 million. And again, to the Chief's point, we're going to work, we're going to continue to work with OMB on that funding level and the headcount level.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 186 Committee on Public Safety
Got it. So, $49.3 million for school crossing guard operations, how much of it goes towards personnel versus other?
That's all personnel costs. And roughly $45.3 million is for the part-time workers and $4 million for the full-time workers.
All right, thank you for that very specific data. All right, so I'll pause here. I'll pass it to the Council Member Phil Wong for a second round of questions.

Thank you, Chairs. The School Safety Agents I met are spectacular. They know the names of every student coming through the doors. They know who they are. They can identify problems before they happen. So I have 100% respect for School Safety Agents. That's where I'm coming from. My question actually is directed to Chief Mary King. Based on the numbers you gave me, there are 1,800 schools in New York City. And currently, your authorized head count is 3,915 School Safety Agents, with 360 vacancies. That means you only have 3,555 School Safety Agents working right now, if everybody shows up every day. You divide that by

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 187 Committee on Public Safety 1,800 schools, which works out to be just around two School Safety Agents per school. Now that's the elephant in the room. The elephant in the room is that when you have a small school, two agents per school is probably adequate. When you deal with the school, a big one with 2,000-3,000 students, there are plenty of high schools. Take any high school, my school, Grover Cleveland, there are over 2,000 students. In the morning, they use what, six entrances? And they use six entrances for dismissal. Two School Safety Agents are clearly inadequate in schools such as Grover Cleveland. And I think that is something that everybody on this panel has to agree with. One, you need more School Safety Agents for large schools, and we have to do better, whether you ask OMB for funds or we ask the Finance Committee for more money to hire them. We don't have enough School Safety Agents based on the numbers you gave me. That is something you could agree with.

Thank you so much for your question. Actually... (CROSS-TALK)

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 188 Committee on Public Safety
Yes or no? Yes or no?

This question, let me elaborate, please. This question is actually giving me the opportunity to update information that I did not provide earlier when I gave the number of total schools. Yes, the total number of schools that we obviously staff is 1,896. However, most of them are co-located, so the number of physical buildings is 1,347.

Okay, you divide that, and it comes out to like three School Safety Agents per school. Now, when you take a high school like Newtown, Maspeth High School, or Grover Cleveland, where there are 2,000-3,000 students, you need more than two or three School Safety Agents. Is this something you agree with?
Absolutely. And they do... (CROSS-TALK)
Okay, so, let’s work... (CROSS-TALK)

and they do... (CROSS-TALK)

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 189 Committee on Public Safety
Let’s work... Let’s admit that... (CROSS-TALK)
and they do... And they do... And they do have the allocation... (CROSS-TALK)
Let’s face this problem... (CROSS-TALK)
for that... (CROSS-TALK)

Let’s face this problem. We admit there is a problem, and let’s work on it. All right? Because we cannot have a solution if there are people here who won’t even admit that we have a problem. All right? We do have a problem. Right? I was outside City Hall protesting when those thousands of School Safety Agents filed for retirement, because they thought they were going to get laid off. All right? So, I know a lot of them left. And I know the numbers. The numbers that you gave me. Numbers that you gave me. We have 1,000 fewer School Safety Agents compared to a couple of years ago. That is a fact. All right?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 190 Committee on Public Safety I am going to get to my question. This is not my question. My question is, Council Member Brewer identified a problem where the kids travel from school to school to school trying to identify kids who may be affiliated with rival gangs. It is happening right now. My district, Grover Cleveland High School, had 18 kids show up last Friday at four o’clock, and fortunately, the doors were closed. If the doors were open, they would go right in. I don’t even know what would have happened. Then, fortunately, the doors were closed, they had video surveillance, and they now know who they are. When I am trying to say that, they moved on to go to other schools on the Brooklyn side. They went to 93, they went to 77, which has far fewer School Safety Agents than Grover Cleveland. So, my question to you is, when you have a graduating class coming in, would you put them in these large schools, because they need more School Safety Agents? Would you do that?

The new class will be deployed to the schools as needed.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 191 Committee on Public Safety
Yes, well, I'm going to tell you now, large high schools, large schools need more School Safety Agents.
Absolutely. And that's...(CROSS-TALK)
Thank you.
that’s something we could always reassess (TIMER)... (CROSS-TALK)
Okay, thank you. That’s it. (CROSS-TALK)
and we will reassess... (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you. That's it. Thank you.

You're hearing a lot, not enough agents, and the idea that they're somehow replaced by a mobile unit just doesn't cut it. It just doesn’t comport with the lived reality of the schools. And I agree, you know, a lot of the big high schools are sharing the concerns with me more than-- elementary schools do, too, but large high schools are as well.

Thank you, Chair.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 192 Committee on Public Safety

You testified before that a school of 3,000 could have one School Safety Agent. That's what you testified to; that was really troubling. You said from one to 10, kind of anywhere from one to 10. I don't think that's a good minimum of one.

And then I clarified that those locations have a minimum of one School Safety Agent for elementary schools. Obviously, as the grade levels go up, and we see the student population at high schools, which is obviously going to be larger, that number fluctuates and will obviously be bigger.
Right. But...
That’s what I stated.

Okay, I accept the clarification; although, it is still not an actual ratio. We still don’t have clarity or a sense of how many School Safety Agents there should be. And the answer is, yes, larger schools should get more. High schools should get more, it's sort of obvious. But we still don’t understand if school... Is the ratio 500:1, is it 1,000:1, is it 3,000:1? We don’t know. We just know that it is not enough. We know, in

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 193 Committee on Public Safety addition to what you said, the 20% (INAUDIBLE) rate, the vacancy rate, and not reporting on it, it is really hard to make headway with this when the numbers are not being reported as per the Administrative Code, and when we are just getting different testimony that is not what we are experiencing in our schools. Again, I was at a school last week, one to two School Safety Agents, and there’s 1,300 kids, two schools. I just don’t see how that is feasible.
Would you be able to share those schools... (CROSS-TALK)

Oh, I am happy to share them with you, and I will invite any principal or teacher to share, publicly, wherever the camera is, to share directly with me. I am happy to share with you. But I am telling you what they are told. They are told that there aren’t enough School Safety Agents, which is true. But it isn’t what you are telling me. You are telling me, “It’s fine. We fill the gaps.” But the gaps are not filled. And there are schools that want to do these afterschool programs, and they have to manage the School Safety Agents, who are told,

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 194 Committee on Public Safety despite what you are telling me, that they have to do forced overtime, and they just have to figure out the schedules. So, I am happy to share those schools with you, if the schools are comfortable doing that.
Please do.

Because I would like to work on these numbers and ratios. And, lastly, I just want to confirm, I know we asked it earlier, but I just want to make sure that the protocols, that the guidance for ICE or non-local law enforcement, the guidance is limited, as I understand it, to activity inside school buildings. But you are saying there are protocols for outside of the building as well?
So anything outside that has the potential to affect schools in any way, schools are trained to activate a GRP activation... (CROSS-TALK)
Right, which includes the perimeters and arrival and dismissal, which includes the... (CROSS-TALK)

It includes the perimeter for arrival and dismissal, right? If we are

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 195 Committee on Public Safety aware of any sighting or enforcement taking place in close proximity to the school perimeter, the school can activate what is called a shelter-in, which is meant to keep all things out.
Yes, I do want to share– I already read it again, but I think...
Mm-hmm?

those protocols need to be shared again, because there is confusion, and there was a directive that there wasn’t clarity, particularly in co-located schools. This was a co-located school. But I have other advocacy organizations where the guidance is not necessarily clear. So, if you are testifying that it is clear, that we have clear guidelines and updated guidance for inside the school building, and on the perimeter, those should be resubmitted to the principals and to school leaders, and to the BRT, so that there is clarity. If you have them, great. Our students need to be safe.

I can absolutely do that. I would really appreciate it, even after, if you can share that particular school with me, so that

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 196 Committee on Public Safety I can go to that school, or have my Borough Safety Director go to the school and walk through with the principal and the co-located leaders, to talk about what transpired, and what they were clear about and not clear about, so that we will have a repeat of that.

Thank you. And, back to the School Safety Agents, I had mentioned in my opening about international schools, schools with a high population of immigrants or non-English speaking language students or their families, uh, is there any consideration when you deploy School Safety Agents to ones that are bilingual or multilingual, going to those international schools, so there can be cultural competency and they can have those conversations with students? Because as much as we love our School Safety Agents, we love our students, and the students told me they love our School Safety Agents, but it has resulted in tensions when there's a language barrier, and it does get very frustrating to the parents who want to see their kids, and there's a language barrier. So, is there consideration given to bilingual School Safety Agents?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 197 Committee on Public Safety

Absolutely. I am the perfect example of that. Having bilingual School Safety Agents when I went through high school was scaring me, and helped me to assimilate into the American mainstream. So yes, absolutely (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)
No, I know that they exist; what I am asking is that we have some schools that are designed to have more bilingual programs. Schools that are designed for newly arrived immigrants... (CROSS-TALK)
We take that in... (CROSS-TALK)
And I am asking if that is part of your deployment strategy?
Absolutely. It is something that we take into account.

Okay. I think there is a lot more work to do there, because there does seem to be miscommunication or a lack of communication. If you are testifying to that, but the schools are reporting that it is not the case, then something needs to be fixed in that line of communication. Because we all want the same thing, we

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 198 Committee on Public Safety want our schools to be safe. We want our School Safety Agents to be respected, as they deserve. And we want our communities to thrive. So I am looking forward to that continued conversation. I am looking forward to-- well, with three hours and 40 minutes of testimony, there is a lot that I am looking forward to — and no answer on 14-150, yet, no? Your quarterly report?
Yes, I am happy to engage with you on that (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)

Yeah, we will have to engage. Because it is required by Local Law, it hasn’t been reported yet on your website, to my knowledge, and that has not been submitted to the Council. So we will certainly continue that conversation. I want to thank the NYPD and the DOE for attending today. This was, I think, a very thorough, a lot of thorough questions about what's going on in our schools and with our School Safety Agents. And, you know, I think we all want the same thing, which is safe schools. And we have to make sure we're on the same page in how we get there. So I want to thank you once again, NYPD. Thank you, uh, New York City

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 199 Committee on Public Safety Public Schools. And this panel is dismissed. Thank you.

And briefly, I, too, want to thank the NYPD and the DOE for being here. I also want to thank all my colleagues who joined us. I especially want to thank the School Safety Agents and the school crossing guards for all the work that they do to keep our students safe, keep them safe inside schools, and also when traveling to and from school. Clearly, there's a lot of work that needs to be done. I'm glad we had this conversation while negotiating this year's budget. These two divisions, the School Safety Agents and the school crossing guards, in my opinion, are two divisions that are grossly underfunded, and I look forward to working with all of you to help resolve some of those challenges. And I think today's conversation was very helpful to that. Thank you for being here.

Okay, for our first panel, I will call up Donald Nesbit, Greg Floyd, and Stamo. She’s like, Cher, it’s just Stamo. You may begin when you are ready. Please state your name for the record. Donald, you may begin.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 200 Committee on Public Safety

Good afternoon, Chairs Dinowitz and Feliz. I am Donald Nesbit, Executive Vice President, Local 372 - NYC Board of Education Employees, District Council 37- AFSCME. It is an honor to come before the Council to speak on behalf of the School Crossing Guards and the vacancies that they have. Local 372 has long testified to the need to hire additional school crossing guards. It is vital in order to keep our children safe from the dangers of reckless drivers and to ensure that school crossing guard members are not stressed by the continuous decline of staff. Student pedestrians also often face major safety traffic hazards every day caused by double and triple-parked cars at bus stops sited in close proximity to our school buildings. School crossing guards are often the first line of defense in ensuring the safety of these students. These workers have risked their own health, safety, and lives to perform vital services to the community, and as the number of school crossing guards continues to decline, thousands of school children cross main intersections without any

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 201 Committee on Public Safety supervision, putting our children's safety in jeopardy. The need for increased protections for our student pedestrians and members of our communities makes it essential for New York City to allocate funding for the additional hiring of school crossing guards. In 2023, former Mayor Adams authorized the elimination of 500 open school crossing guard positions, completely eliminating the hiring of additional school crossing guards. There have been a number of casualties since. For example, in March of 2024, an 8-year-old boy died in Queens after being struck just five blocks from school. In February of this year, an 11-year-old girl was killed while crossing the street in Brooklyn. Just yesterday at DC 37, we celebrated Krystyna Naprawa, a school crossing guard who was killed on Woodhaven Boulevard and Atlantic Avenue (TIMER) in 2023. I have just a little bit more.

Yes, finish your thought, of course.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 202 Committee on Public Safety

By eliminating these open positions and not hiring additional school crossing guards, the City sends a dangerous message: The safety of our children in New York City is not the City’s priority. Local 372 respectfully requests that the City restore these 500 open positions and hire additional School Crossing Guards, providing our school children with heightened protection as they travel to and from school. Again, thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony before the Council.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chairs Dinowitz and Feliz, and Members of the Council. I am Stamo Karalazarides, First Vice President at The Council of School Supervisors and Administrators. I am here today on behalf of our President, Henry Rubio, and our CSA leadership. School safety is one of the most urgent issues facing our schools right now. When students don't feel safe, nothing else works. Instruction suffers, families lose confidence, and school leaders are pulled away from teaching and learning to manage crises.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 203 Committee on Public Safety What we're seeing on the ground is a real shift over the last few years. Students are coming into schools with higher levels of anxiety and stress. Families are more worried than ever about bullying, social media conflicts, mental health, and violence both inside and outside of school buildings. At the same time, we have far fewer Safety Agents than we did before the pandemic. And despite that, thousands of dangerous items, including firearms, are still being intercepted in our schools each year. The risk is real, and the staff we have are doing the critical work, but we don't have enough of them. We're also asking school leaders to do more with less. This is where the role of assistant principals becomes critical. Assistant principals are often the first responders inside a school. When there's a fight, a medical emergency, or a student in crisis, they're the ones stepping in immediately. They coordinate with Safety Agents, support teachers, communicate with families, and stabilize situations in real time. But beyond emergencies, they’re also doing the daily work that prevents those situations from happening in the first place: Monitoring school climate, addressing conflicts early, supporting

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 204 Committee on Public Safety struggling students, and keeping systems running smoothly. Right now, dozens of schools are operating without an assistant principal. That creates a real gap. It means fewer trained leaders available in critical moments, slower response times, and less capacity to prevent before they escalate. As class size reductions bring more teachers into buildings, the need for leadership doesn't stay the same; it grows. Without corresponding increases in supervisory staff, we're putting more pressure on fewer people to manage increasingly complex environments. But the bigger issue is that our system is still mostly reactive. We respond after incidents happen instead of preventing them. If we're serious about safety, we need to invest in prevention, mental health supports, counseling, and restorative practices. Right now, those supports are inconsistent and often insufficient. We also need to fix systems that unintentionally (TIMER) make things worse, like safety transfers that move challenges from one school to another without proper information or support.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 205 Committee on Public Safety The path forward is clear: Restore staffing, strengthen leadership, ensure technology works, and shift towards prevention. Safety isn't just about responding to incidents; it's about building school environments where those incidents are less likely to happen in the first place. Thank you.

Thank you so much for your testimony. When you mentioned safety transfer, it just reminds me that the easiest way to get transferred out of a school is to get beaten up. Just a weird way to run a school system. Chair Feliz?

Thank you very much. Thank you both for being here and also for all the important work that you do to support school crossing guards and our School Safety Agents. My question is for Donald, uh, specifically about school crossing guards. I know you and your team have conversations very often with school crossing guards. What would you say are the top issues that you think we should work on to make life better and easier for these crossing guards? I know you mentioned a higher headcount. What do you

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 206 Committee on Public Safety think would be an appropriate number? And also salary, I don't think anybody would disagree that $19.00 an hour is poverty wages, and that is beyond unacceptable. Based on your conversations with crossing guards and the stakeholders, what do you think would be a fair salary for these crossing guards?

So, one, I believe restoring the number to the 2,500 headcount. What we saw with Krystyna Naprawa on Woodhaven and Atlantic, where she was struck by the truck, wasn't only that there weren’t any signs or visibility. Those were issues, but she was the only one there. We repeatedly said, on corners of this magnitude, if you have ever been to Woodhaven and Atlantic, you know that's not a normal corner or intersection. You need multiple school crossing guards at all four of those corners. A lot of our schools have school crossing guards where there are multiple corners of a school, yet there's one school crossing guard on one intersection, where students are traveling from several different corners to get to school. So restoring their headcounts would be the priority.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 207 Committee on Public Safety In terms of salary and pay, we've done multiple things in increasing the whole-- we think of our members as holistic members. So there were plenty of issues, uh, the City, during the summertime, when the school crossing guards didn't work, they didn't have health insurance like every other City worker while being off. We had to testify before panels to increase, and now every school crossing guard's health insurance is covered year-round. We created the Level II position that you heard about today. The Level II position was created because they were going to give other members of the Police Department supervision over a school crossing guard while performing other duties. And police officers at the time couldn't do it. So we created a Level II as a promotional path for school crossing guards. So, a full-time school crossing guard, which by the way is the only full-time school crossing guard anywhere in the US, we created that position so they can have a promotional path towards a full-time position as a school crossing guard. So that was something that we actually created. But there's a need for more in terms of school crossing guards. Quick example, if there's a

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 208 Committee on Public Safety snow day related to schools, schools are closed, the school crossing guards do not get paid, right? They do not get paid for the day.
Right. Right.

It just doesn't make any sense. If they're closely related to schools like everyone else, they should be compensated for the day. So there's multiple things and we continue to make the life of a school crossing guard better, But, I would say there's a lot-- And lastly, I'll just say that safety equipment and materials, what we've learned and studies have shown, school crossing guards that are hit on the impact from a car, their head material, most of them die from head trauma. So safety material to keep them protected, and their lives protected, is important.

Thank you. Thank you so much for the information. And a similar question regarding School Safety Agents, what do you think would be the proper headcount? I know you mentioned that technology is crucial, but if there aren't enough agents to use the technology, then we won't be able to get the safety

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 209 Committee on Public Safety that we need inside our school. So, what do you think would be the proper headcount? And anything on technology? Do we need additional technology?

Regarding the number of Safety Agents that we need in school, it would be nice if we could come up with a ratio for a student: safety agent. Certainly, we need, at a minimum, what we had before the pandemic, which was approximately 5,200. We need at minimum that amount. Also, I just want to bring to your attention that the attrition rate is that we're losing approximately 25 to 30% of our SSAs each year. So we do not have enough SSAs coming into our school buildings to keep our students safe. That attrition rate is simply unsustainable. And high schools with large populations who have multiple SSAs don't have enough SSAs, don't have what they had before the pandemic, and very, very, very frequently, I would say daily, have their SSAs pulled from their buildings to cover those absences, which we were told today are 20%. So we're looking at about 30% less than the pandemic and 20% absences every day. The numbers don't lie.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 210 Committee on Public Safety
Were you surprised by the 20% number?

I do hear of a lot of absences each day. And our school leaders frequently don't know someone's absent until the beginning of the day when they arrive at school. And then they have to wait for an agent to come. So we've had complaints where our leaders are waiting sometimes until 11:00 a.m., or even noon, for a Safety Agent to come in.
Mm-hmm. And they testified that when they have those absences, they have those mobile units. Can either of you talk about your reaction to hearing that testimony?

So, as the person who worked in a school building, like yourself, Councilman, we understand that the mobile units respond to situations, especially with a reduction in headcount; they respond to serious situations throughout the city. And so once you place them in a school, let me just take a step back-- the Assistant School Safety Agent was put in place because, as CSA has testified to, you know, the principal is waiting, so they put a parent coordinator or a school aide.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 211 Committee on Public Safety And in terms of safety, we as a union said, well, our members are not trained tactically to even be at a desk, right? So if someone comes in and is looking to do harm to folks within the school building, our members are not trained like a School Safety Agent to protect folks. And we're going to do whatever we have to do to protect folks, like everyone in the school community. But we need that level of training. So the creation of the Assistant School Safety Agent was just in response to the Union pushing back for the safety of our school aides who may be there, or someone else. But let me say principals have to do what they have to do to protect the school building...
Yeah.
Right? And so we never blame them for doing what they need to do. We just say that the safety is still in question when someone is there who’s not tactically trained to do the job.
